title: Trump Sued Over Truth Social’s $100,000-a-Month Early-Access Feed
description_medium: On August 12, 2026, The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation sued President Donald Trump, federal officials and Trump Media over Truth API, a paid feed offering early access to posts from ten prominent Truth Social accounts, including Trump’s. The service charged up to $100,000 per month. The complaint asked the court to stop the White House from distributing official announcements exclusively through the feed; these are plaintiffs’ claims, not a ruling.
description_long: Truth Social’s parent company, Trump Media & Technology Group, launched Truth API on August 1, 2026. The paid data feed offered subscribers access to posts from ten high-profile accounts, including President Donald Trump’s, before the posts became available to the public. Reporting described the highest price as $100,000 per month. On August 12, The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed suit in Manhattan federal court against Trump, White House officials and Trump Media. The complaint argued that selling earlier access to official government announcements could violate constitutional protections and asked the court to prevent the White House from posting those announcements exclusively through the paid service. The litigation raised questions about whether public presidential communications could be monetized through a private company in which Trump has a financial interest, and whether a paid feed could give subscribers a market-sensitive timing advantage. Those points are allegations and concerns raised in the lawsuit; they are not findings that the service violated the law. The plaintiffs later sought a preliminary injunction. The suit challenged the paid access model and its relationship to government communications, rather than simply the sale of ordinary social-media data.
evidence_notes: Reuters and Yale Law School identify plaintiffs, Aug. 12 filing, service launch, up-to-$100,000 monthly price, high-profile accounts, and requested relief. Plaintiffs moved for preliminary injunction Sept. 4; describe constitutional claims as allegations.
corrected_wording: Reframed API as Truth API and specified the lawsuit’s actual demand concerning exclusive White House announcements. Changed generic legal accusation into attributed plaintiffs’ claims.

title: FinCEN Exempts U.S. Companies From Beneficial-Ownership Reporting
description_medium: On August 11, 2026, the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final rule permanently exempting U.S. companies and U.S. persons from reporting beneficial-ownership information under the Corporate Transparency Act. The rule took effect August 14 and directed FinCEN to delete previously submitted information about exempt U.S. persons. Certain foreign entities still must report information about foreign owners. Treasury called the change a small-business burden reduction.
description_long: The Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issued a final rule on August 11, 2026, permanently removing the Corporate Transparency Act’s beneficial-ownership reporting requirement for U.S. companies and U.S. persons. The rule took effect on August 14. It made permanent exemptions that FinCEN had adopted on an interim basis in 2025 and directed the agency to delete previously reported information it reasonably identifies as belonging to U.S. persons. Beneficial-ownership reports are intended to identify the individuals who ultimately own or control companies, information that authorities can use in investigating money laundering and other financial crimes. Under the final rule, certain foreign companies registered to do business in the United States remained reporting companies and must report information about foreign beneficial owners. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described the rule as a reduction in regulatory burdens for small businesses and said it would not compromise national security. The change therefore narrowed the reach of the federal ownership database rather than abolishing every reporting obligation for every company connected to the United States. The title “Win for Dark Money” states an advocacy judgment; this account describes the agency action and scope of the exemption without treating that characterization as a formal finding.
evidence_notes: Treasury/FinCEN final-rule announcement gives effective date, exemptions, data deletion and remaining foreign-entity obligations. Attribute rationale to Treasury; the short title is an advocacy characterization.
corrected_wording: Replaced “Win for Dark Money” with the specific rule change. Clarified that U.S. entities/persons became exempt while certain foreign reporting companies remain subject to reporting.

title: Trump Defends Family Business Interests in CNBC Interview
description_medium: President Donald Trump discussed his family’s business dealings and a recent Supreme Court ruling during an Oval Office interview with CNBC’s Joe Kernen on July 2, 2026. He said his children handled his finances and defended the family’s cryptocurrency venture. He also praised a June 29 ruling that upheld his firing of Federal Trade Commission member Rebecca Slaughter, saying it gave the president more power. Those remarks do not resolve the underlying ethics questions.
description_long: CNBC anchor Joe Kernen interviewed President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on July 2, 2026. The discussion included Trump’s family businesses and potential conflicts of interest, his family’s cryptocurrency venture, the Supreme Court, the economy and other policy subjects. Asked about his financial interests, Trump said his children handled his investments and defended the family’s business activity. The interview followed financial disclosures that prompted questions about income from Trump-affiliated ventures. Trump rejected the idea that the business arrangements were improper. Kernen also asked about the Supreme Court’s recent decision in Trump v. Slaughter. On June 29, the Court ruled 6–3 that statutory limits on the president’s ability to remove Federal Trade Commission commissioners were unconstitutional, upholding Trump’s removal of Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter. Trump described the result as giving the presidency more power. That case concerned control of an independent agency and the scope of presidential removal authority; it did not adjudicate the legality of Trump family business dealings. This entry records Trump’s defense and the interview’s subjects, rather than treating his assertions as an independent determination that conflicts were absent. It also distinguishes his comments about the FTC ruling from the court’s legal holding.
evidence_notes: CNBC/VERSANT transcript identifies interview and date; Senate transcript copy supplies full remarks. Supreme Court opinion in Trump v. Slaughter and contemporaneous reporting establish the June 29 ruling. Keep Trump's self-defense attributed.
corrected_wording: Corrected the alleged interview’s title and identified the specific FTC removal decision. The linked source in the frozen entry was unrelated and has been replaced with CNBC and primary records.

title: Salon Analysis Says Trump’s New Tariffs Could Raise Consumer Costs
description_medium: A Salon commentary published August 16, 2026, argued that newer U.S. tariffs were designed to last longer than the temporary duties struck down by the Supreme Court and that overlapping levies could raise costs for consumers. It described new tariffs under trade statutes covering forced labor, national security and discrimination against U.S. imports. The piece cited economic estimates and reflected the author’s analysis; it did not establish a single final consumer cost.
description_long: In an August 16, 2026, Salon commentary, trade economist Kent Jones argued that a set of newer tariffs could impose lasting costs on U.S. consumers. The article distinguished these measures from the broad “Liberation Day” tariffs that the Supreme Court had struck down earlier in the year. Jones said the administration’s newer levies rested on other statutory authorities, including Section 301, Section 232 and Section 338, and could be layered on top of existing duties. He cited estimates from the Dallas Federal Reserve and Yale Budget Lab suggesting that tariffs had contributed to higher prices and that consumers bore a substantial share of the cost. The article also described levies on selected goods and countries, including 10%–12.5% rates linked to the administration’s forced-labor investigation. Its “forever tariffs” phrasing and interpretation of tariffs as an instrument of personal power are the author’s analysis, not the text of a single executive order. The piece explains why the author expected cumulative costs to persist; actual prices depend on product, country, business decisions and subsequent policy changes. It does not establish that consumers pay every tariff in full or that every announced duty would remain unchanged.
evidence_notes: Salon identifies Kent Jones’s analysis, tariff authorities and cited estimates. Attribute “forever” and personal-power interpretation to the author; costs vary across goods and levies and should not be stated as a single determined consumer payment.
corrected_wording: Changed the categorical claim that consumers are footing a settled bill to an attributed forecast about cost pass-through and stacked tariffs. Corrected category implication by focusing on trade policy rather than election interference.

title: CBS News Maintains a Rolling Collection of Trump Investigation Coverage
description_medium: The linked CBS News feature is a rolling collection of separate reports, not a dated inventory of every investigation involving Trump. Its entries cover distinct federal and state matters, including Jack Smith’s investigations, the New York hush-money case and later proceedings. Because the page combines events from different years and procedural stages, it cannot establish which probes remained active on a single date.
evidence_notes: CBS page consists of a changing list of dated stories. The packet does not define which inquiries to count or provide a fixed status date, and the rolling page mixes concluded investigations, litigation about past investigations and new probes.
corrected_wording: Changed title to describe the cited page accurately as continuing coverage rather than asserting a complete inventory of ongoing investigations.
exact_blocker: No fixed cutoff or defined set of investigations is supplied, and the CBS feature is a rolling page with entries at different procedural stages; it cannot substantiate the title’s plural claim that investigations were ongoing on a single date.

title: White House Email Becomes Evidence in Colorado Retaliation Lawsuit
description_medium: In August 2026, Colorado cited a December 15, 2025, email from White House official Emily Underwood in its lawsuit alleging federal retaliation over the state’s treatment of Tina Peters and its election policies. The message invited officials from five agencies and OMB to discuss “immediate actions” regarding Colorado. State lawyers argued it showed coordination; the White House disputed a connection to Peters. A judge ordered further records produced as the case proceeded.
description_long: Colorado’s lawsuit against the Trump administration alleged that federal actions against the state were retaliation connected to its election policies and the prosecution of former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters. In an August 11, 2026, discovery hearing, the state presented a December 15, 2025, email sent by White House official Emily Underwood. The message called on officials at five federal agencies and the Office of Management and Budget to join a conference call and discuss immediate actions their departments could take with respect to Colorado. State attorneys described the email as evidence that actions affecting the state were coordinated after Trump attempted to pardon Peters, who had been convicted under state law. The White House disputed that the call related to Peters. The Justice Department did not contest the email’s existence but argued that the Executive Office should not have to produce additional records. The judge largely granted Colorado’s discovery request and ordered more information released as litigation continued. The email documents that a White House staffer convened agencies to discuss action concerning Colorado; by itself, it does not establish that Trump authored the message or directed each later funding or policy decision. The state’s claim of a broader retaliation scheme remained a contested allegation in the lawsuit.
evidence_notes: CBS Colorado reports the Aug. 11 hearing, Underwood email, parties’ positions and discovery result. CPR and Sen. Bennet’s statement corroborate the email and allegations. Distinguish documented email from state’s inference about Trump’s personal direction.
corrected_wording: Removed the unsupported assertion that the email directly links Trump personally to the campaign. Described its actual contents, Colorado’s allegation and the discovery ruling.

title: DOJ Legal Opinion Says Executive Privilege Can Cover Trump’s Private Advisers
description_medium: On August 10, 2026, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion saying a president may assert executive privilege over certain confidential communications with private advisers outside government. The memo emerged amid litigation over Trump administration orders targeting law firms and could affect a subpoena for outside adviser Boris Epshteyn. Harvard law professor Noah Feldman argued in a syndicated opinion that the theory was unprecedented and legally unsound.
description_long: The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel issued a 21-page opinion on August 10, 2026, concluding that executive privilege may cover some confidential presidential communications with private advisers who do not work for the federal government. The opinion said the communication must concern official presidential decision-making, involve the president or a direct adviser, and remain confidential. The memo mattered in ongoing litigation over executive orders that targeted several law firms and agreements made with others. The American Bar Association alleged that the administration had used government power to pressure firms because of their legal work, hiring practices, diversity policies or political ties. In that case, the government argued it should not have to identify advisers involved in developing the orders, and the opinion could affect efforts to obtain testimony or communications from outside adviser and lawyer Boris Epshteyn. Harvard law professor Noah Feldman, writing in a Bloomberg Opinion column syndicated by the Sydney Morning Herald, criticized the theory as a major expansion of executive secrecy and warned it could blur the boundary between public and private advice. That criticism is legal commentary, not a court ruling. The cited event is the OLC’s legal position and its potential role in litigation, not a judicial decision that the privilege applies to every outside adviser.
evidence_notes: CBS describes Aug. 10 OLC opinion and criteria; Reuters details assertion in ABA litigation over law firm orders and Epshteyn. SMH/Bloomberg Opinion is Feldman’s critique, not a legal ruling.
corrected_wording: Reframed the sensational title as a report about DOJ’s OLC opinion and attributed the “grab for power” assessment to columnist Noah Feldman.

title: Colorado Courts Challenge Trump Administration Actions Against the State
description_medium: A Colorado Sun opinion column published August 17, 2026, argued that state and federal courts had impeded parts of Trump’s effort to pressure Colorado over Tina Peters. It cited an email convening federal agencies to discuss actions concerning the state and court orders in disputes over voter data and related matters. The column’s “retribution tour” framing is the author’s conclusion, while the email and court proceedings are documented events.
description_long: In an August 17, 2026, opinion column, Colorado attorney Mario Nicolais argued that court proceedings had checked parts of the Trump administration’s campaign against Colorado. He linked that argument to the state’s refusal to transfer Tina Peters, a former county clerk convicted in a state election-equipment case, into federal custody and to Trump’s symbolic claim that he had pardoned her. The column discussed a December 2025 White House email organizing a call with federal agencies to discuss immediate actions concerning Colorado. In a separate dispute over voter data, a federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking unredacted Colorado voter records, finding the government had not shown a sufficient legal basis for access. Nicolais also described funding decisions and other federal actions as retaliation against the state. Those characterizations are his opinion; Colorado’s broader retaliation case was still being litigated, and the email alone does not prove that Trump personally directed every agency action. The column’s central argument was that courts and state officials had resisted attempts to use federal power in response to Colorado’s handling of Peters and elections. This entry therefore treats “retribution tour” as the columnist’s framing and distinguishes it from the underlying email, court cases and state-federal disputes.
evidence_notes: Colorado Sun marks the item as opinion and identifies the columnist’s interpretation. CPR reports Aug. 4 dismissal of DOJ voter-data suit; CBS details the separate email and discovery dispute. Do not conflate those proceedings or present the retaliation inference as a judgment.
corrected_wording: Replaced the sweeping slogan title with the court actions the opinion addresses. Attributed “retribution” to the columnist and distinguished the two separate lawsuits.

title: Colorado Challenges Trump Administration Actions in Court
description_medium: Colorado officials challenged multiple Trump administration actions through federal litigation in 2026, including demands for state voter data and new federal program rules. A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s suit for unredacted Colorado voter records in August, while the state joined other lawsuits over separate policies. The disputes cover distinct legal issues, so a broad claim that every action was illegal or retaliatory should remain attributed to the sources making it.
description_long: Colorado’s attorney general tracked dozens of federal lawsuits filed or joined by the state against Trump administration policies. The disputes concerned separate subjects rather than one coordinated case. In August 2026, a federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s suit seeking unredacted Colorado voter data, ruling that the government had not adequately explained its need for the records. Earlier that month, Colorado also joined challenges to federal policies involving human-services funding and tariffs. In another lawsuit, the state alleged that federal actions were intended to punish Colorado over its election policies and treatment of former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters. Colorado cited a White House email inviting agencies to discuss immediate actions regarding the state; the administration disputed the state’s account of the email’s purpose. These events illustrate a continuing federal-state legal conflict, but they have different parties, statutes and procedural outcomes. A dismissal in the voter-data case does not decide the legality of unrelated rules or establish that every policy was retaliatory. The underlying source for this entry does not identify the specific measures behind its claim that federal efforts against Colorado were “unprecedented” or “likely illegal.” The supported description is therefore a concise account of the litigation portfolio and examples with explicit attribution to Colorado’s filings.
evidence_notes: Colorado AG tracker documents the state’s litigation portfolio; CPR reports dismissal of the voter-data suit; Colorado Politics covers TANF and tariff suits; CBS reports allegations and email in a distinct retaliation case. Attribute unlawful/retaliatory claims.
corrected_wording: Replaced broad unsupported “unprecedented/likely illegal” language with separate examples and their procedural status, distinguishing allegations from rulings.

title: DOJ Announces Plan for 1,000 Monitors at 2026 Midterm Polls
description_medium: Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon announced in August 2026 that the Justice Department planned to send about 1,000 federal monitors to polling places for the November midterms, a record number for the department. DOJ said monitors would observe compliance with federal voting laws; deployment locations had not yet been fully announced. The plan followed decades of DOJ monitoring, but drew scrutiny amid the administration’s voter-roll lawsuits and Trump’s election rhetoric.
description_long: In August 2026, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said the Justice Department planned to deploy approximately 1,000 federal monitors to polling places during the November midterm elections. The announcement concerned a planned deployment, not a completed nationwide operation. DOJ has long sent staff to observe compliance with federal voting protections. The department reported that 289 people were sent to polling places in the 2022 midterms and 714 people monitored 86 jurisdictions across 27 states in the 2024 presidential election. The 2026 plan would be larger than those recent efforts; the department said it expected to recruit federal employees, including staff from U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, and that the locations would be announced after primaries concluded. DOJ also announced monitors for primary elections in Miami-Dade County, Florida, and Laramie County, Wyoming. The effort came as the Civil Rights Division was pursuing lawsuits for unredacted voter data from states, including Colorado; judges had blocked requests in many of those cases. The division said its work aimed to ensure accurate voter rolls, while states and voting-rights advocates expressed concern about federal involvement in election administration. The reporting does not establish that the monitors were intended to influence election outcomes. The distinction between longstanding observation and the unusually large planned count is central to the story.
evidence_notes: CBS News gives Dhillon’s announcement, historical counts and recruitment/status details; Democracy Docket and Washington Post corroborate plan. The account says planned, not deployed, and omits unsupported claim that purpose was to sway courts or Congress.
corrected_wording: Changed “deploys” to “announces plan”; removed claim of intent to sway courts or Congress and explained lawful monitoring context and contemporary concerns.
